cards.title: Excavate the job with timeline interviews, not feature wish lists
cards.summary: Asking recent buyers to draw their decision timeline surfaces the emotional obstacle that features and surveys miss.
cards.use_when: You have traffic but poor conversion, or focus groups keep returning feature requests that don't move sales.

cards.title: Use Jobs Theory as an integration tool for fragmented research
cards.summary: Jobs Theory tells you which pieces of existing research matter and how they fit together, without discarding your data.
cards.use_when: You already have personas, focus groups, panels and competitive analysis but they don't produce clear innovation direction.

cards.title: Five recurring questions to audit every offer
cards.summary: A reusable audit checklist drawn from the jobs framework to test whether your offer is built around a real job.
cards.use_when: Running a positioning, offer or roadmap review and needing a structured set of challenge questions.

cards.title: Define the Market by Job, Not Product or Customer Category
cards.summary: Re-framing the market around the customer's Job to Be Done reveals growth where product- or demographic-based categories show none.
cards.use_when: You are sizing a market, prioritizing a roadmap, or suspect your category definition is hiding demand (e.g., an ecommerce brand defining itself by product type instead of the progress customers want).

cards.title: Drill Deep and Look Wide: Functional, Emotional, Social Dimensions
cards.summary: A job has functional, emotional and social dimensions; innovations that only address the functional miss context and fail.
cards.use_when: You are defining requirements for a product, page, or experience and want to avoid the common trap of solving only the functional dimension.

cards.title: Don't Do Design Requirements in a Conference Room — Go Into the Wild
cards.summary: Asking experts what they want in a conference room misses the real job; observe people in the actual circumstances where they use the product.
cards.use_when: You are gathering requirements from internal stakeholders, power users, or customers via interviews and need to validate that stated needs match real behavior.

cards.title: Study Nonconsumers and Workarounds for High-Potential Jobs
cards.summary: People who buy nothing (not even from competitors) and people inventing workarounds often reveal the richest unmet jobs.
cards.use_when: Your growth has plateaued with current customers and you want to find new demand outside your existing base.

cards.title: Distinguish the Big Hire from the Little Hire
cards.summary: Most data tracks the purchase (Big Hire) but ignores the moment of consumption (Little Hire), which determines whether the product really solves the job.
cards.use_when: You are measuring product-market fit, retention, or why downloads/purchases don't translate into repeat use.

cards.title: Map the Four Forces: Push, Pull, Inertia, Anxiety
cards.summary: Two forces drive change (the push of the situation and the pull of the new solution) and two block it (habits of the present and anxiety about the new); all four must be understood.
cards.use_when: You are designing for conversion or adoption and want to reduce friction, not just add appeal.

cards.title: Reduce Switching Anxiety, Not Just Increase Appeal
cards.summary: Innovators over-focus on making the new solution attractive and under-focus on the anxieties that block people from switching.
cards.use_when: You have a strong offer but adoption/checkout is stalling, or you are launching a new or trust-sensitive product type.

cards.title: Identify What Must Be Fired for Your Product to Be Hired
cards.summary: Every hire requires firing the current solution — including doing nothing; companies under-consider what their product replaces.
cards.use_when: You are launching or repositioning and need to understand the real competition and switching cost.

cards.title: Storyboard the Customer's Struggle to Reveal Competing Forces
cards.summary: Sketch the customer's struggle as a narrative (Pixar-style beats) to surface pushes, pulls, anxieties and context.
cards.use_when: You need to convert interview or observation notes into a structured narrative of a decision, or design an onboarding/purchase experience around real moments.

cards.title: Run a Documentary-Style Job Interview on Circumstances, Not Features
cards.summary: A JTBD interview reconstructs a timeline of the purchase decision from the first thought, focusing on circumstances, not product features.
cards.use_when: You are interviewing recent buyers/purchasers to understand why they really chose you, and standard feature-preference surveys aren't giving usable answers.

cards.title: Read the Mattress Case: Clues in Circumstances, Not Features
cards.summary: In the Mattress Agenda interview, the real story was pain, spousal conflict, warranty frustration, and store anxiety — not coil count or firmness.
cards.use_when: You want a concrete model of how an apparently simple, impulse-looking purchase conceals a long, complex job when you gather circumstances.

cards.title: Watch for Unusual Product Use as a Job Clue
cards.summary: How customers use your product — especially in unexpected or unusual ways — reveals the real job better than their stated preferences.
cards.use_when: You are mining customer behavior or support data and want to spot jobs you aren't currently designing for.

cards.title: Use Your Own Life as a Legitimate Source of Job Insights
cards.summary: The book's takeaways include that personal experience is a valid, rich source of JTBD insights — many successful innovations came from introspection.
cards.use_when: You are stuck for insight or want a low-cost way to start identifying jobs without launching a full research program.

cards.title: Focus on Cause, Not Luck, in Innovation
cards.summary: The JTBD lens treats innovation as a search for cause — asking what will cause what — so breakthroughs don't depend on lucky accidents.
cards.use_when: You are framing an innovation or experimentation program and want to argue for hypothesis-driven search over hoping for a lucky find.

cards.title: Signal 'This Is Not for You' to Avoid Alienating Wrong-Fit Buyers
cards.summary: If a customer hires your product for reasons other than its intended job, they may later call it a bad product; signaling who it's not for protects you.
cards.use_when: You have a strong niche offer and are tempted to broaden messaging to grab more buyers, or you're getting mismatched customers who churn or complain.

cards.title: B2B Jobs Still Carry Emotional and Social Weight
cards.summary: Even constrained B2B procurement decisions involve anxiety, reputation, career risk and habits of the present.
cards.use_when: You sell to businesses/teams and are tempted to treat the purchase as purely rational or functional.

cards.title: Reframe 'Good Enough' as a Jobs Question, Not an Opinion
cards.summary: Judgments of whether a product is good enough are unresolvable without a Job to Be Done to anchor them.
cards.use_when: Your team is stuck arguing whether a feature, page, or offer is 'good enough' and the debate keeps cycling.

cards.title: Big Hire vs Little Hire: Separating Purchase from Continued Use
cards.summary: Distinguish the moment a customer buys a product (Big Hire) from the repeated moments they actually use it (Little Hire), and treat both as separate jobs to be won.
cards.use_when: Evaluating why a product sells but churns, or why purchase data looks healthy while usage or retention lags

cards.title: Storyboarding the Switch: Push, Pull, Inertia and Anxiety
cards.summary: Build a rich storyboard of the customer's circumstances and struggles, capturing the four forces that push customers toward or hold them back from a new solution.
cards.use_when: Designing qualitative customer research, mapping a purchase journey or choosing which friction to remove first

cards.title: Depth over Breadth: Why Fewer, Richer Interviews Beat Large Samples
cards.summary: Collect many data points per person from a small sample instead of a few data points from a huge sample, because innovation insight comes from depth rather than breadth.
cards.use_when: Designing qualitative research, deciding between a survey and interviews, or when quantitative data shows patterns without explaining them

cards.title: Writing a Job Spec: From Customer Job to Design Blueprint
cards.summary: Translate a multifaceted customer job into an innovator-side spec covering functional, emotional and social dimensions, tradeoffs, competitors and obstacles.
cards.use_when: Moving from customer research to product, offer or experience design for a new or repositioned product

cards.title: Competing with Nonconsumption and Unlikely Alternatives
cards.summary: Identify the real competitive set by looking at what customers hire instead of your product, including workarounds, adjacent categories and doing nothing.
cards.use_when: Doing competitive analysis, category positioning or identifying barriers to adoption in a low-penetration market

cards.title: Selling Experiences, Not Features: The Resume That Gets You Hired
cards.summary: Create the right set of purchase and use experiences around a clearly defined job so the product's 'resume' earns the hire, which is harder for competitors to copy than features.
cards.use_when: Differentiating in a category where features are easily copied, or justifying a premium price

cards.title: Structuring the Business Around Jobs Instead of Demographics
cards.summary: Organise products, stores and processes around a shared job rather than a demographic segment, which produces experiences competitors cannot easily reverse-engineer.
cards.use_when: Reconsidering audience segmentation, store or site structure, or how to defend against copycat competitors

cards.title: Designing Against Anxiety: Anticipating Objections Before the Purchase
cards.summary: Actively design experiences that defuse the anxieties blocking a purchase, especially spouse approval, disposal of the old product and fear of choosing wrong.
cards.use_when: Reducing pre-purchase hesitation on considered purchases such as furniture, mattresses or high-ticket items

cards.title: Reviews as Job-Matching Evidence
cards.summary: Understand that online reviews work by letting buyers find reviewers who share their job, and manage reviews as a two-sided asset that also tells wrong-fit customers not to buy.
cards.use_when: Optimising product pages, managing marketplace reputation, or deciding what review content to surface

cards.title: Building a Purpose Brand Around One Job
cards.summary: Aim for a purpose brand that becomes synonymous with a specific job, which produces price premiums, recall without heavy advertising, and protection from disruption.
cards.use_when: Developing brand positioning, naming a product line, or deciding whether to extend a brand into new categories

cards.title: Avoiding Feature-Only Research: What Traditional Panels Miss
cards.summary: Traditional panel and survey research reveals functional preferences but misses the experiences and obstacles that determine whether customers actually adopt a solution.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a research plan that relies mainly on doctor or expert panels, feature-preference surveys or disease/behaviour statistics

cards.title: Recognising an Insight: It Feels True on Conception
cards.summary: A genuine jobs insight lands as intuitively true and is contrarian, seeing something others have missed; in hindsight it seems obvious, but it rarely was.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a research finding is a real insight worth building on or just an interesting data point

cards.title: Using Job Research to Generate Retail and Marketing Hypotheses
cards.summary: Convert depth interviews into testable hypotheses about store staffing, couple engagement, partnerships and advertising rather than jumping to conclusions from one interview.
cards.use_when: Turning qualitative job research into a prioritised roadmap of experiments for a retailer or brand

cards.title: Jobs Theory and Design Thinking as Complementary Approaches
cards.summary: Jobs Theory supplies the causal explanation and language for customer insight, which complements design thinking's emphasis on empathy, divergent thinking and rapid iteration.
cards.use_when: Reconciling an existing design-thinking or human-centred design process with jobs-based research

cards.title: Purpose brand: own a job, not a category
cards.summary: Integrate the brand around one clear Job to Be Done so customers think of you automatically, instead of becoming a price-competing category placeholder.
cards.use_when: Deciding brand positioning or evaluating whether feature/benefit expansion is diluting what the brand stands for

cards.title: Write a job spec before designing the solution
cards.summary: Capture the full richness of the customer's job in a job spec covering functional, emotional and social dimensions, tradeoffs, competitors and anxieties, then use it as the innovation blueprint.
cards.use_when: After customer research has surfaced a job and you need to translate it into requirements for a product, service or experience

cards.title: Treat every complete solution as a service
cards.summary: Even product companies must design the full experience of purchase and use, because a complete solution to a job always functions like a service.
cards.use_when: When your product is strong but customers still struggle to buy, onboard or get value from it

cards.title: Integrate processes around the job, not the org chart
cards.summary: Competitive advantage comes from proprietary cross-functional processes that deliver the customer's job, and large reorganizations usually fail to create that value.
cards.use_when: When restructuring seems like the answer to growth or execution problems, or when functions deliver in silos

cards.title: Shift complexity from the customer to your processes
cards.summary: Job-aligned processes should absorb the nuisance work customers would otherwise do themselves, leaving them with positive experience and progress.
cards.use_when: When customers abandon or stall because of friction such as paperwork, coordination or repeated follow-up

cards.title: Measure customer-benefit metrics, not internal activity
cards.summary: Replace internal financial and activity metrics with externally relevant measures of whether the customer's job got done.
cards.use_when: When dashboards full of conversion, retention or cost metrics don't explain whether customers are actually succeeding

cards.title: Process optimization needs a job-alignment factor
cards.summary: Efficiency alone can make you better at the wrong things; optimize processes for efficiency and alignment with the customer's job.
cards.use_when: When process improvement, automation or cost reduction is underway and you need a criterion beyond throughput

cards.title: Use subroutines to make process reuse deliberate
cards.summary: Instead of informally sharing best practices, identify repeatable process modules that can be reused wherever the same operation is needed.
cards.use_when: When scaling operations across regions, product lines or channels and each team reinvents the same steps

cards.title: Start every innovation from the job-spec press release
cards.summary: Frame a new offering by writing the customer-facing announcement first, so experience and process decisions derive from the job it will be hired to do.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a new product, feature or service, especially when engineering or channel ownership is fragmented

cards.title: Give the customer's job an internal owner
cards.summary: Assign stewardship of end-to-end job delivery, because functions and product lines rarely have anyone accountable for the customer's job.
cards.use_when: When customers experience a broken journey across handoffs and each function believes it is doing its job

cards.title: Run meetings focused on the job to avoid politics
cards.summary: A recurring cross-functional forum centered on the customer's job gives diverse specialists a shared language and prevents debate from collapsing into opinions and turf.
cards.use_when: When cross-functional teams argue from their own professional backgrounds instead of solving the customer's problem

cards.title: Beware stack fallacy when moving into adjacent solutions
cards.summary: Technical strength in your layer does not mean you understand the customer one level up, so moving up the stack requires first-hand empathy for that customer's context.
cards.use_when: When considering a product extension or new service built on your existing technology or supply strength

cards.title: Find the job in moments of struggle, not feature lists
cards.summary: OnStar initially bundled cool features as brochure ware, but the real job emerged only when the team listened to actual customer calls at moments of crisis.
cards.use_when: When your product has many features but customers churn because they don't need most of them

cards.title: Repeat time-consuming research at each execution stage
cards.summary: Features and collateral are not enough when a growing team loses touch with customer reality; direct exposure to real interactions must be repeated as the company scales.
cards.use_when: When a growing organization is making decisions from data and internal assumptions rather than customer contact

cards.title: Build process flexibility to match faster technology cycles
cards.summary: When your delivery technology iterates much faster than your host industry's validation cycle, create deliberate mid-cycle processes or you will ship outdated versions.
cards.use_when: When your product depends on rapidly improving technology embedded in a slow-moving hardware, channel or regulatory environment

cards.title: Make channel incentives a process design problem
cards.summary: A dealer or partner whose economics don't reward selling your offering can quietly kill it, so design the channel process and incentive around the job.
cards.use_when: When a partner or channel is the front line of purchase and your offering is a small share of their revenue

cards.title: Take responsibility for customer business outcomes
cards.summary: Shift from selling training modules or tools to owning the customer's transformation, and spend R&D on process innovation that shifts complexity away from the client.
cards.use_when: When your category is vulnerable to budget cuts because clients see it as a discretionary product purchase

cards.title: Diagnose your organization's immune system
cards.summary: Unchanged processes and local resource-allocation habits can reject a validated idea before it ships; treating process change as an immune response helps you plan for it.
cards.use_when: When a research-backed improvement keeps dying in implementation despite good evidence

cards.title: Use the job spec to review experiences and obstacles
cards.summary: The source's leader questions turn a job spec into an audit of whether current solutions address every detail, obstacle and stage of the customer's experience.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a product line, customer journey or growth plan against the job you believe you are hired for

cards.title: The Three Fallacies of Innovation Data
cards.summary: Growing companies drift from customer jobs because operators fall for three data traps: active-vs-passive data, surface growth, and conforming data.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a once jobs-focused ecommerce brand now chases product lines, channel metrics or exec pet projects instead of customer progress.

cards.title: Passive Data Needs Active Management
cards.summary: The context-rich signal that reveals a job has no voice, structure or champion, so leaders must deliberately give it a standing role in decisions.
cards.use_when: Setting up research cadence and decision rights so customer-job evidence survives contact with the operating dashboard.

cards.title: Surface Growth vs. Solving the Core Job Better
cards.summary: Copying competitors' products or piling new jobs onto the same customers grows revenue on paper while diluting the job that won the customer.
cards.use_when: Evaluating catalog expansion, brand extension, line extensions or acquisition of adjacent product lines before committing.

cards.title: Conforming Data: Why You Miss the Obvious
cards.summary: Each function brings data that supports its own incentives, and decision 'leaps' are often pre-skewed before the meeting starts.
cards.use_when: Running innovation, range or investment reviews where sales, marketing, product and finance all present supporting numbers.

cards.title: All Data Is Made by Someone with an Agenda
cards.summary: Numerical precision hides judgment: financials, big-data models and surveys all embed human choices about what to count.
cards.use_when: Choosing or defending a data source for a positioning or product decision, or when a team treats dashboards as ground truth.

cards.title: Jobs as the Unit of Analysis: TurboTax's Shift from Interview to Done
cards.summary: Reframing from the product's internal component to the customer's desired outcome unlocks creativity and a clearer roadmap.
cards.use_when: When feature requests and backlog items pile up but no one can say which ones matter, or a core product step has become the optimization target itself.

cards.title: Four Organizational Benefits of a Jobs Focus
cards.summary: Jobs clarity pays off in decision autonomy, resource allocation, culture and measurement — four distinct levers, not one vague morale boost.
cards.use_when: Making the internal business case for adopting jobs-based language, or auditing which of the four benefits is actually missing.

cards.title: Why Mission Statements Fail as Daily Guides
cards.summary: Generic mission statements inspire but cannot arbitrate daily tradeoffs; a specific job spec can.
cards.use_when: When a company has a mission or purpose statement that nobody can translate into product, service or merchandising decisions.

cards.title: Two-Sided Compass: Using the Job to Decide What Not to Do
cards.summary: A clear job definition narrows options productively — deciding what does not belong as much as what does — and speeds crisis decisions.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing a service, feature or benefit roadmap where everything looks technically feasible and marketable.

cards.title: Make Jobs the Common Language Across Functions
cards.summary: A one-syllable phrase gives marketing, engineering, sales and service a shared reference point instead of talking past each other.
cards.use_when: Cross-functional planning sessions where each department optimizes its own metrics and meetings end without alignment.

cards.title: Leader Questions to Audit Jobs-Centeredness
cards.summary: A reusable question set reveals whether the customer's job is genuinely guiding product, marketing, service and investment decisions.
cards.use_when: Running a quarterly strategy or innovation review, or onboarding a new functional leader, to test alignment around customer progress.

cards.title: Levitt and Drucker: The Drill-vs-Hole Disconnect
cards.summary: Customers buy solutions to problems, yet company behavior usually reveals a product-defined self-image — the core gap Jobs Theory addresses.
cards.use_when: Teaching or re-anchoring a team on customer-centric framing before writing positioning, roadmaps or campaign briefs.

cards.title: Use a Job Statement as an Alignment Compass
cards.summary: A clearly articulated job statement acts as a two-sided compass: it aligns both the customer's problem and the internal job spec, enabling autonomous employee decisions.
cards.use_when: When an ecommerce team's roadmap or feature debates lack a shared anchor, or when employees need to make day-to-day tradeoffs without escalation.

cards.title: Jobs Focus Produces Four Organizational Benefits
cards.summary: An organization explicitly focused on a well-defined job enjoys distributed decision making, resource optimization, inspiration, and better measurement.
cards.use_when: When making the business case for job-based positioning, or when restructuring teams, budgets or KPIs around customer jobs.

cards.title: Culture Built on the Job Enables Unprompted Action
cards.summary: When employees deeply understand the job, they clear roadblocks on their own; the leader's role is to build structures that let those choices happen.
cards.use_when: When designing customer-service or support empowerment policies, or when deciding how much discretion front-line staff should have.

cards.title: Replace Generic Mission Statements with Job Statements
cards.summary: A well-crafted statement of the jobs a company exists to solve can be both inspiring and practical, unlike generic mission statements.
cards.use_when: When rewriting a company mission, vision or internal rallying cry so it actually guides decisions.

cards.title: Measure What Improves Customers' Lives, Not Just What's Easy
cards.summary: Companies tend to measure easily captured data and miss whether they are improving customers' lives; measure the job-relevant outcome instead.
cards.use_when: When choosing KPIs or analytics dashboards for an ecommerce business, or when data is abundant but feels disconnected from customer value.

cards.title: Amazon-Style Job Metrics with Automatic Price Adjustment
cards.summary: Amazon anchors its retail business on three customer job measures — vast selection, low prices, fast delivery — monitored minute by minute and treated as defect-free requirements.
cards.use_when: When designing monitoring and enforcement systems for a core customer promise such as price competitiveness or delivery speed.

cards.title: Separate the Distinct Jobs a Product Is Hired For
cards.summary: Traditional products often bundle several different customer jobs and do none well, hiding what people actually hire them to do.
cards.use_when: When an established product or channel is losing ground and you need to decide which jobs to double down on and which to abandon.

cards.title: Use Functional, Emotional and Social Lenses on the Job
cards.summary: Define a job through its functional, emotional and social dimensions, since customers often hire a solution for the emotional payoff on top of a functional task.
cards.use_when: When writing positioning or creative strategy and the functional benefit alone doesn't explain customer attachment.

cards.title: Segment by Job, Not Demographics
cards.summary: A segment can be large, distinct and underserved yet invisible to demographic and psychographic segmentation because it is defined by a shared job.
cards.use_when: When demographic or psychographic segments aren't producing differentiated messaging, or when a promising audience seems 'unfindable' by standard targeting.

cards.title: Watch for Organizational Drift Away from the Job
cards.summary: As companies grow, the organizing unit shifts from the customer's job to internal processes, products, competitors and investors, creating an edited view of the customer.
cards.use_when: When a scaling ecommerce business's processes, org chart or reporting feel increasingly detached from what customers want.

cards.title: Validate a Job Statement by Abstraction Level
cards.summary: A valid job statement is expressed in verbs and nouns and can be solved by candidates from multiple, different product categories.
cards.use_when: When checking whether a job statement is genuinely a job, or when a team's 'job' is really a preference, a spec or an aspiration.

cards.title: Demand Matrix: Classify an Idea by Price vs. Customer Volume
cards.summary: Back-of-napkin framework that sorts a product idea into high-end, golden goose, mass market, or the unprofitable labor-of-love quadrant.
cards.use_when: You have a rough product or offer idea and need a fast sanity check on whether it can be profitable before investing in research or creation.

cards.title: Google Competitor Scan to Index Sub-Markets and Framing
cards.summary: Use basic Google searches on problem keywords to catalog competitor sites and read their imagery, tone, and headlines for distinct sub-niches.
cards.use_when: You are starting qualitative research on a new niche and need to see who already sells to this market and how they frame themselves.

cards.title: Read Competitor Headlines for Pain, Constraints and Promise
cards.summary: Extract the buyer constraints and desired speed of results encoded in competitor promises ('25 minutes for an hour's results').
cards.use_when: Analyzing competitor landing pages or sales copy to infer what kind of buyer each promise is written for.

cards.title: Amazon 3-Star Review Mining for Structural Gaps
cards.summary: Filter to middle reviews to find recurring product criticisms and structural gaps rather than emotional buying triggers.
cards.use_when: You want to know what a category's existing books or products fail to deliver, so you can design around known shortcomings.
